habitat: Dry grassland, hedge banks, field margins and rough sunny ground
blurb: A bushy cottage-garden mallow that flowers for three solid months in soft rose-pink (or pure white), over finely cut leaves that smell faintly musky when crushed. Easy, bee-covered and short-lived — it keeps itself going by seeding around.
water: Moderate; deep weekly soak in summer heat
spread: Bushy and upright; self-seeds freely and maintains itself that way
seasons: Rose-pink or white saucers June–September; finely divided musk-scented foliage; brown seed 'cheeses' into fall
wildlife: Bees and butterflies work the flowers heavily

care.hardiness: Rated USDA zones 3–8, so winter cold is no obstacle here at zone 5b–6a. Heat is the bigger limit: NC State notes foliage can yellow in hot, dry weather, which on the Front Range means it looks best with some afternoon relief in July and August.[1][2]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, in average well-drained soil. It transplants easily as a young plant — there is no deep taproot to fight — and it does perfectly well in a large container given regular water, though it is short-lived enough that most gardeners simply let it reseed in the ground.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun gives the sturdiest, best-flowered plants; NC State also allows partial shade (2–6 hours), and a little afternoon shade is genuinely helpful in our high-altitude summer sun.[2][1]
care.soil: Average, medium, well-drained soil. NC State records it on clay, loam or sand at a neutral pH of about 6.0–8.0, which covers essentially all Front Range garden soil, and it tolerates moist ground as well as occasional dryness.[2][1]
care.water: Medium. Give it a deep soak about weekly through summer heat — this is not a xeric plant, and drought shows up first as yellowing, tired foliage. It is not a water hog either; ordinary border watering suits it.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space 15–18 in apart. Plants are bushy but narrow, and a group of several reads far better than one, since each individual is short-lived.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, and it does the work itself — both MBG and NC State note it self-seeds freely in suitable positions and maintains itself that way. Because it is a short-lived perennial often grown as a biennial, sowing seed rather than dividing clumps is the practical approach.[1][2]
care.sow: Sow outdoors in late summer or fall for flowers the following year, or start indoors in early spring for a first-year bloom. Seedlings transplant readily while small.[1][2]
care.bloom: June to September in 1.25 in rose-pink flowers with five notched, wedge-shaped petals around a small central column of stamens; there is also a clean white form. Both flowers and foliage are musk-scented, most noticeably when bruised.[1]
care.maintenance: Remove spent blooms to keep it flowering — MBG makes deadheading the key task, and it genuinely extends the season here. Cut the plant to the ground after frost, and leave a few seedheads if you want next year's replacements. Staking is rarely needed at this height.[1]
care.selfsow: It self-sows freely. That is how a short-lived plant persists, but it does mean seedlings turn up where you didn't plant them — deadhead before the ring-shaped seed 'cheeses' dry if you want it contained. It has naturalized widely across North America, so keep it out of wild land, though it is not a listed noxious weed in Colorado.[1][2]
care.troubles: Generally pest- and disease-resistant. Japanese beetles are the usual nuisance, foliage may yellow in hot dry spells, and it can pick up foliar disease in crowded, humid conditions — space plants for airflow and water at the base rather than overhead.[1][2]

edible.card: Young leaves, flowers & green seeds in salads
edible.summary: Leaves and flowers are a documented addition to wild salads, and the green seeds are edible too — mild, mucilaginous and pleasant rather than strongly flavoured.[2]
edible.caution: NC State documents the leaves and flowers as salad additions and the seeds as edible; use the young leaves, since older ones turn coarse and hairy, and eat the ring-shaped green seed 'cheeses' while still soft rather than dry and brown. Everything mallow is mucilaginous, so a large helping is slimy and mildly laxative — treat it as a garnish, not a green. Only eat plants you know have not been sprayed, and don't take it from roadsides, where mallows readily colonize contaminated ground. Anyone with a known mallow-family sensitivity should avoid it. Confirm your plant is *Malva moschata* by its finely cut, musk-scented leaves before eating any part.[2][1]
